title: The Resolved Brief
subtitle: A guided walkthrough that captures what your family would actually need.

sections.title: Foundation & Legal
sections.subtitle: The documents that determine whether your wishes are followed.
sections.intro_message: We'll start with the basics — the documents that determine whether your wishes are followed or whether the state makes those choices for you. If you have these in place, we'll capture where they live. If you don't, we'll note it as pending. At the end, you'll have a chance to handle each pending item — either now or with your Action Plan.

questions.prompt: How confident are you that, if something happened tomorrow, your family would actually know what to do — not just have access to the documents, but know how to use them?
options: Very — we've talked through it and everything is current
Pretty confident — but we haven't reviewed things in a while
Honestly, I assume we're mostly there but I haven't pressure-tested it
We have some things in place but I know there are gaps
questions.follow_up_tip: Almost everyone has the components — will, insurance, accounts. The question we're going to answer over the next 30 minutes is whether the components actually fit together into something your family could use under stress.

questions.prompt: Do you have a current will?
options: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it
questions.follow_up_tip: More than half of American adults don't have a will. We'll capture where you are and route the path forward through your Action Plan.

questions.prompt: When was your will last updated?

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.follow_up_tip: Wills written when life looked different often don't reflect who or what you'd want now.

questions.prompt: Where is your will physically located?
questions.placeholder: e.g. home safe, attorney's office, safe deposit box

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.follow_up_tip: The most common gap isn't whether a will exists — it's whether the family can find it when they need it.

questions.prompt: Who is your estate attorney, if you have one? (Name + phone)
questions.placeholder: e.g. Patricia Chen, 415-555-0142

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.prompt: Who is currently named as the executor in your will, if you've named one? (Name + phone)
questions.placeholder: e.g. James Thompson, brother — 312-555-0142

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.follow_up_tip: If the executor named is someone you no longer trust or have a relationship with, this is a priority update for your will.

questions.prompt: If your will names a guardian for your children, who is it? (Name + phone)
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mark and Rachel Davies — 214-555-0190

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.follow_up_tip: Wills written when kids were small often don't get updated. Verify this name still makes sense for the life you live now.

questions.prompt: Are the executor, guardian, and beneficiaries named in your will still the right people for the life you live now?

show_if: Yes — and it reflects my current situation
Yes — but it's been a while since I reviewed it

questions.follow_up_tip: Wills are time capsules; they don't auto-correct. If anything has changed — divorce, new children, deaths, fallouts — the will needs to be updated.

questions.prompt: Do you have a Financial Power of Attorney — someone authorized to make financial decisions if you can't?
options: Yes — formally documented and they know
Yes — but they may not know the details
I think so, but it's not written down
questions.follow_up_tip: The financial POA is different from the medical proxy and different from the executor. It covers what happens if you're alive but unable to act.

questions.prompt: Do you have a Healthcare Power of Attorney or medical proxy?
options: Yes — formally named and we've discussed what I'd want
Yes — formally named, but we haven't gotten into specifics
Someone would step in by default, but it's not documented
questions.follow_up_tip: Without a formal healthcare proxy, hospitals follow state default rules. That works when everyone agrees — and creates a court issue when they don't.

questions.prompt: Where do your important legal and financial documents live?
options: One consolidated location (home safe, attorney's office, etc.)
Mostly in one place but a few are scattered
Not sure where some of them are
questions.follow_up_tip: The right answer is the one where someone could find everything in under an hour. Consolidation isn't aesthetic — it's operational.

questions.prompt: What locations are involved?

show_if: Mostly in one place but a few are scattered
Not sure where some of them are

questions.prompt: Beyond documents — does someone have physical access to your home, vehicles, and any safes? Keys, codes, combinations?
options: Yes — at least one trusted person has keys/codes for everything
Partial — they have some access but not all
questions.follow_up_tip: Documents and physical access are paired. The Action Plan will include a path to document physical access. Specifics — codes, combinations, key locations — go in your Resolved Companion Document.

questions.prompt: Which professional advisors do you currently work with?
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. We'll surface contact info for each — the people your family would actually call.

sections.title: Key People & Decision Makers
sections.subtitle: The people who'd step in for you — and whether they're actually ready.
sections.intro_message: You may have the documents. The question this section answers: are the people named in them actually ready to do the job? By the end of this section, your Brief will have a complete contact list and a clear chain of command — so when someone has to step in, they know who they are, what they're responsible for, and who to call.

questions.prompt: If something happened tonight, who is the ONE adult who should walk in and start running things? Name + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Sarah Brennan, sister — 312-555-0167
questions.follow_up_tip: This is different from your medical proxy or executor. This is the person who handles operations: gets the kids, finds the Brief, makes calls.

questions.prompt: Have you told this person — out loud, in plain words — that they are this person?
options: Yes — clearly named and they've agreed
We've discussed it but I haven't formally said 'you are this person'
They probably assume it, but we've never talked about it directly
questions.follow_up_tip: Naming someone in a document and telling them are two different things. The Action Plan will include a script for the conversation.

questions.prompt: When your Brief is delivered, will this person know where to find it?
questions.follow_up_tip: The Brief only works if your point person can find it. Tell them the exact location — a drawer, a safe, a folder.

questions.prompt: If your primary point person had to act in the first 48 hours — funeral home, executor calls, immediate decisions — how prepared are they?
options: Very — they're competent and we've talked through it
Competent, but I'm not sure they'd know what to do first
Capable, but they'd be flying blind on logistics
questions.follow_up_tip: Your Brief will include a 'First 48 Hours' page with the practical sequence — what to do, in what order, with phone numbers.

questions.prompt: If your primary point person was also unavailable, who is the backup? Name + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Tom Hernandez, friend — 415-555-0193
questions.follow_up_tip: The backup is the person who steps in if the primary can't. Could be a sibling, a close friend, your executor — whoever can pivot fast.

questions.prompt: If you and your spouse/partner were both unavailable, is there clarity on who steps in?
options: We have ideas but it's not formal
Not applicable — only one adult in the household
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. We'll flag this in your Action Plan with a framework for thinking it through if it's incomplete.

questions.prompt: Is it clear which person handles which domain? Legal, financial, medical, funeral logistics — different people often handle different parts.
options: Mostly clear but some overlap or ambiguity
Not really clear — same name on everything
questions.follow_up_tip: Your Brief will include a 'Roles & Responsibilities' page that assigns each domain explicitly — legal, financial, medical, funeral logistics, day-to-day. Generated from your answers so far.

questions.prompt: Your Brief documents your wishes — funeral preferences, asset decisions, medical directives. But there's a category of execution decisions the Brief can't anticipate: which funeral home, when to hold the service, how to handle a thousand small choices in the first months. For those — is there one person whose word is final?
options: Not applicable — only one person involved
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. Tiebreaker authority covers execution decisions the Brief doesn't address.

questions.prompt: If your family had to speak for your wishes — funeral preferences, medical decisions, what you'd want done with your stuff — how confident are you they'd get it right?
options: Mostly — they'd have direction but might guess on specifics
They'd be guessing on most of it
questions.follow_up_tip: The rest of this interview captures your wishes in your own words. By the time you finish, your family will have your actual answers, not their best interpretation.

sections.title: Children & Dependents
sections.subtitle: The people who depend on you — and who steps in for them.
sections.intro_message: This section captures the practical things — who steps in, how their lives continue, what they need — and then the things only you can give them. Take your time on this one. Your progress saves automatically. Come back tomorrow if you need to.
sections.skip_prompt: Do you have minor children or other dependents?

questions.prompt: Names and ages of your dependents (children, parents in your care, anyone who relies on you day-to-day).
questions.placeholder: e.g. Lucy (14), Jake (11), Emma (8) — and my mother Carol (76) who lives with us
questions.follow_up_tip: Include anyone whose daily life depends on you being there.

questions.prompt: Is there a documented plan for who would raise your children if both parents were gone?
options: Yes — formally named in our will, and they know
We have ideas but no decision
questions.follow_up_tip: Most parents with minor children don't have a documented guardian. We'll prioritize this in your Action Plan if needed.

questions.prompt: Permanent guardian — as named in your will. Name + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mark and Rachel Davies — 214-555-0190
questions.follow_up_tip: If your will doesn't name a guardian, write 'Need to add' here. The Action Plan will surface this as a priority.

questions.prompt: Does this permanent guardian know they've been named — and agreed to it?
questions.follow_up_tip: If they haven't said yes, they may say no when it matters. The Action Plan will include a conversation script.

questions.prompt: Temporary guardian — the person who picks up your kids THAT NIGHT if both parents are unavailable. Name + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Sarah Brennan, sister — 312-555-0167
questions.follow_up_tip: This is the operational answer. Not the legal long-term guardian — the person who shows up at school by 4pm tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Can this temporary guardian actually get into your house? Key, code, smart lock app — whatever it takes.
options: Yes — they have a physical key
Yes — they have the entry code
Yes — they're on the smart lock app
questions.follow_up_tip: Most homes today are a mix — front door code, smart lock for guests, garage keypad. What matters is that they have at least one reliable way in.

questions.prompt: Could someone in your life drive your vehicles tomorrow if they needed to?
options: Yes — they have keys/fobs and know where they're kept
Yes — they're on the car's app (Tesla, BMW Connected, FordPass, etc.)
questions.follow_up_tip: Modern cars increasingly require app access or a paired phone. Spare keys aren't always enough. Specifics go in the Companion Document.

questions.prompt: Have you put your temporary guardian on the school / daycare's authorized pickup list — in writing?
questions.follow_up_tip: Schools require this paperwork in writing. Verbal agreements won't get a child released. The Action Plan will include a reminder to update the form.

questions.prompt: What does whoever takes over need to know that only you know? Medications, allergies, routines, fears, comforts, the small things.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Lucy is allergic to peanuts (EpiPen in kitchen drawer). Jake takes ADHD meds at 7am with food. Lucy's therapist is Dr. Kim, Tuesdays 4pm. The dog needs his arthritis pill at bedtime.
questions.follow_up_tip: The boring details are the important ones. Be specific.

questions.prompt: What values, traditions, or things would you want them to carry forward? You don't have to write this perfectly — just whatever comes to mind.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Sunday dinners. Reading together at bedtime. Being honest, even when it's hard. Not taking themselves too seriously.
questions.follow_up_tip: Your Brief will hold this in your own words. The guardian gets the practical instructions and the why behind them.

sections.title: Money, Assets & Obligations
sections.subtitle: The map of what you have and what flows through.
sections.intro_message: Quick note before we start: we're not asking for account numbers, balances, or passwords. None of that lives in your Brief, ever. Those details belong in your Resolved Companion Document — a separate document you'll download at the end. You can fill it in digitally, print it and write by hand, or both. Whichever you prefer. It stays with you — we never see it. What we're capturing here is the map. Where things live. Who to call.

questions.prompt: If something happened tomorrow, who could access cash to handle the first week?
options: Spouse only — but only on their own accounts
A trusted person has signature authority on at least one account
Family would have to figure it out — potentially hit walls
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. We'll capture your bank info now and flag the access path in your Action Plan.

questions.prompt: Which banks or credit unions do you use? Just the names.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Chase, Schwab, Local Credit Union

questions.prompt: Across all your accounts, which types do you have?
options: Joint accounts with someone other than spouse

questions.prompt: What retirement accounts do you have? (Select all that apply, or 'None'.)
Where are these accounts held? Just institution names.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Fidelity (401k), Vanguard (IRA)

questions.prompt: Old 401(k)s or retirement accounts from PREVIOUS employers — list anything you remember, even if you're not sure where they are now.
questions.placeholder: e.g. 401(k) from Acme Corp (2018-2021), old IRA at company that got acquired by Salesforce
questions.follow_up_tip: Forgotten 401(k)s are a common gap. The Action Plan will include the lookup tools your family would use to track them down. Listing the employer is enough to start.

questions.prompt: Any investment or brokerage accounts outside retirement?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Schwab brokerage, Robinhood, Public.com

questions.prompt: Where does your income come from?
Bills on autopay — which ones, and what account or card do they hit?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mortgage (Chase checking), utilities (Chase Sapphire), insurance (Wells Fargo checking)

questions.prompt: Bills you pay manually (not on autopay)?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Property taxes, quarterly estimated taxes, water bill, condo fees
questions.follow_up_tip: Manual bills are easier to miss. The Action Plan will include a path to consolidate or automate where possible.

questions.prompt: Which credit or debit card is most of your autopay running off of?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Chase Sapphire ending in 4521
questions.follow_up_tip: If this card expires, gets replaced, or gets cancelled, every autopay attached to it will start failing. Your family needs to know which card holds everything together.

questions.prompt: When does that card expire? (Month / year)
questions.follow_up_tip: Set a calendar reminder for 60 days before expiration. Update the card on file with every recurring billing relationship.

questions.prompt: Any loans? (Mortgage, car, student, personal, business.)
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mortgage with Wells Fargo, car loan with Chase, student loans with Nelnet

questions.prompt: Property, vehicles, and valuables your family might overlook?
questions.placeholder: e.g. storage unit in Dallas, jewelry in home safe, classic car at uncle's garage, second property
questions.follow_up_tip: The obvious things (house, car) are easy. What's worth capturing is what they'd miss — storage units, collections, second properties, items held elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Do you have a safe deposit box?
Which bank, and who has the key?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Chase Main St branch, spare key in desk drawer
questions.follow_up_tip: Without the key, getting into a safe deposit box requires a court order.

questions.prompt: Do you own a business, hold an ownership stake, or have significant intellectual property?
options: Yes — and there's a formal succession plan
Yes — but no formal succession plan
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. If there's no succession plan, we'll flag this as a priority in your Action Plan with paths to working with a business attorney or CPA.

questions.prompt: If your spouse or executor had to take over your finances tomorrow, how prepared are they?
options: Very — they could pick it up
Mostly — they know the basics but not all the specifics
Not applicable — no one else involved in finances
questions.follow_up_tip: If the answer is 'they'd be lost,' two paths beyond what's in your Brief: a walkthrough call with a Resolved specialist where we sit down with you and your spouse together, or an introduction to a financial advisor. Both will be in your Action Plan.

sections.title: Insurance & Protection
sections.subtitle: What you have, where it lives, who gets it.
sections.intro_message: We're going to capture what you have, identify any gaps, and put together a review list. Some of these might be quick fixes. Some might be worth a conversation with a professional. Either way, you'll know where you stand by the end.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your life insurance — is it through work, private, or both?
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. We'll come back to coverage adequacy once we have a fuller picture.

questions.prompt: Provider(s)?
questions.placeholder: e.g. State Farm (private), MetLife (work)

questions.prompt: Approximate coverage amount?
questions.placeholder: e.g. $500K work + $1M private

questions.prompt: Who is the PRIMARY beneficiary?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Spouse, Sarah Brennan

questions.prompt: Who is the CONTINGENT (backup) beneficiary?
questions.placeholder: e.g. children equally per stirpes, sibling, trust
questions.follow_up_tip: If the primary beneficiary is unable to receive the payout, the contingent does. Without one, the policy goes through probate. For parents with minor children, the right contingent structure depends on your situation — the Action Plan will surface this for review with an attorney or financial advisor.

questions.prompt: When did you last review the beneficiary designations on this policy?
options: Never reviewed since I bought it
questions.follow_up_tip: Stale beneficiary designations are one of the most common gaps a review catches. If your life has changed — marriage, divorce, kids, deaths — the wrong person may still be named.

questions.prompt: Disability insurance?
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. Coverage varies significantly between policies. The Action Plan will include a review item if relevant.

questions.prompt: Long-term care insurance?
options: I have assets that would cover LTC
Significant impact on family if needed
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. The Action Plan will include LTC frameworks if relevant to your situation.

questions.prompt: Home or renter's insurance?
questions.placeholder: e.g. State Farm policy #...

questions.prompt: Auto insurance?
questions.placeholder: e.g. GEICO

questions.prompt: Any other policies? (Umbrella, business, liability.)
questions.placeholder: e.g. $2M umbrella through Chubb

questions.prompt: Insurance agent or broker — primary contact?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mike Diaz at Brown & Brown — 415-555-0167

questions.prompt: Have you reviewed beneficiary designations across ALL your accounts and policies — life insurance, retirement accounts, transfer-on-death accounts — in the last few years?
questions.follow_up_tip: Beneficiary designations override your will. The Action Plan will include the audit checklist organized by institution type.

sections.title: Digital Life & Access
sections.subtitle: The phone, email, and passwords that gate everything else.
sections.intro_message: In 2026, your digital life IS your life. If your family can't get into your phone or email, they can't do anything else. Sensitive specifics — passwords, codes, recovery phrases — go in your Resolved Companion Document. We'll capture the map here.

questions.prompt: Could your family get into your phone if needed?
options: Yes — at least one trusted person has the passcode
Yes — biometric access works for someone in the household
Probably — but it's never been tested
No — only I can unlock it
questions.follow_up_tip: The phone passcode itself goes in your Companion Document. The Brief notes the access path.

questions.prompt: Will you add your phone passcode to your Companion Document?
options: Yes — and biometric backup info if applicable
I'll figure out a way to share access another way

questions.prompt: Could your family get into your computer?
options: No — only I can log in
questions.follow_up_tip: As long as your account password is documented on your Companion Document, your family can access the computer the same way you do.

questions.prompt: Email is the master key — most password resets and statements route through it. Let's capture each email account that matters. Start with your primary, then any others (work, secondary, specialty).
questions.placeholder: e.g. john.doe@gmail.com (primary), jdoe@workcompany.com (work), johndoe1985@yahoo.com (old/recovery)
questions.follow_up_tip: Most adults have 3–5 email accounts. The Brief captures which exist; credentials go in your Companion Document.

questions.prompt: How would your family access your primary email account?
options: It's saved in our shared password manager
They'd use the provider's recovery process

questions.prompt: Does your primary email have 2-factor authentication (2FA) enabled?
questions.follow_up_tip: 2FA is great security — but if your family only has the password, they still can't get in. They need the second factor too.

questions.prompt: Where are your 2FA backup / recovery codes stored?
options: I'll add them to my Companion Document
Stored on my phone (which they can access)
I haven't set up backup codes
questions.follow_up_tip: Every 2FA system generates backup codes when you set it up. If you didn't save them, you can regenerate them in your account settings. This is one of the highest-leverage Companion items.

questions.prompt: How do you manage your passwords?
Which password manager do you use?
Where will the master password or access method be stored for your family?
options: Emergency access feature inside the manager itself
questions.follow_up_tip: The master credential is the single most important item on your Companion Document — it unlocks everything else.

questions.prompt: Where are your photos stored?
Important documents in cloud storage?
Financial apps on your phone your family should know about?
Do you have any cryptocurrency?
Which platform, and where is the recovery phrase stored?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Coinbase, recovery phrase in fireproof safe
questions.follow_up_tip: Crypto recovery phrases are unique — if lost, the assets are unrecoverable. Specifics go in your Companion Document.

questions.prompt: Subscriptions the household needs to keep running — and ones that can be cancelled. Anything come to mind?
questions.placeholder: Keep running: Wi-Fi, Netflix (kids), iCloud storage, kids' cell plans. Cancel: my gym, industry tools, premium services I used alone.
questions.follow_up_tip: Most households have 20–40 active subscriptions. Some are critical, some are personal. The Companion Document has a longer worksheet — start with what comes to mind here.

sections.title: Medical & Final Wishes
sections.subtitle: What you'd want — and how you want to be remembered.
sections.intro_message: Last section. This one's about the part most people put off the longest — what you'd want in the final stretch, what you want your family to know, and how you want to be remembered. There's no rush here. Some of these questions need a minute. If you need to pause, your progress saves. What we capture in this section becomes some of the most useful pages of your Brief — and probably the most meaningful.

questions.prompt: If you couldn't speak for yourself — accident, illness, anything that took your voice away — who is making medical decisions? And do they know it?
options: Yes — formally named, and we've discussed what I'd want
Formally named, but we haven't gotten into specifics
Someone would step in by default, but it's not documented
questions.follow_up_tip: Without a formal healthcare proxy, hospitals follow state default rules. The Action Plan will include a path forward — most states have free standard forms.

questions.prompt: Healthcare proxy — Name + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Sarah Brennan (spouse), 312-555-0167

show_if: Yes — formally named, and we've discussed what I'd want
Formally named, but we haven't gotten into specifics

questions.prompt: Does this person know they've been chosen — and what you'd want?
options: Yes — but we haven't gotten into details
I named them but haven't told them

show_if: Yes — formally named, and we've discussed what I'd want
Formally named, but we haven't gotten into specifics

questions.follow_up_tip: Naming a healthcare proxy and preparing them are two different things. The Action Plan will include a medical wishes conversation script.

questions.prompt: Backup person if they're unavailable?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Tom Hernandez (sibling), 415-555-0193

questions.prompt: If you were in a state where machines were keeping you alive with no realistic chance of recovery — coma, severe brain injury, end-stage organ failure — what would you want?
options: No life support — let me go peacefully
Time-limited trial — try for a defined period, then withdraw if no improvement
Continue life support as long as possible
I'd want my proxy to decide based on the situation
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. Your Brief will document this in plain language that a hospital can act on.

questions.prompt: If you have a living will or advance directive document, where is it physically located?
questions.placeholder: e.g. home safe, with my attorney, in the file cabinet labeled 'Medical'
questions.follow_up_tip: A directive only works if it can be found. Your healthcare proxy needs to know where to look.

questions.prompt: If your heart stopped and CPR was an option — what would you want?
options: Yes — unless I'm already in late-stage terminal illness
My proxy decides based on the situation

questions.prompt: Organ and tissue donation — are you registered as a donor, and is that what you want?
options: Yes — registered, want everything donated that can be
Some donations only — want my proxy to know my preferences

questions.prompt: Primary care doctor — Name + practice + phone.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Dr. Patel, Bayview Medical, 415-555-0123

questions.prompt: Specialists you see regularly?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Dr. Kim (cardiologist), Dr. Stevens (endocrinologist)

questions.prompt: Health insurance provider?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Blue Cross PPO, employer-provided

questions.prompt: Where is your insurance card?
If you were brought to a hospital unconscious tomorrow, could someone tell the doctors what they need to know — conditions, medications, allergies?
options: Yes — my spouse or family knows the basics
Some details would be available; others would be guesswork
My family doesn't really know my medical situation in detail
There isn't much medical history to know
questions.follow_up_tip: The Brief captures your physicians and broad categories. The specifics — medications, dosages, allergies — go in your Companion Document.

questions.prompt: Disposition preferences?
options: Haven't decided — let my family choose

questions.prompt: Any specific location preference? (Cemetery, scattering location, etc.)
questions.placeholder: e.g. Mountain View Cemetery, plot already purchased

questions.prompt: Service preferences?
options: No service — small family gathering only
Nothing — I don't want a service
Let my family decide what works for them

questions.prompt: Anything you specifically don't want? Religious elements, songs, speakers, an open casket, a long church service — no judgment on any of it.
questions.placeholder: e.g. No open casket. No church service. Please not 'Amazing Grace.'
questions.follow_up_tip: The clearer this is, the easier the day is on your family.

questions.prompt: Anything you specifically do want? A song, a reading, a specific person to speak, a tradition to honor.
questions.placeholder: e.g. My brother gives the eulogy. Play 'Landslide' by Fleetwood Mac. Everyone wears bright colors.
questions.follow_up_tip: Captured. The funeral preferences page is one of the most-read pages of the Brief, because families want to honor wishes and worry about getting it wrong.

questions.prompt: Anyone who should be notified that your family might not think of?
questions.placeholder: e.g. Old college roommate Jamie Park, mentor Bill Reston, ex-coworker Susan Diaz

questions.prompt: Take a moment with this one. Beyond the practical stuff — beyond the documents, the proxies, the wishes — how do you want to be remembered? Not 'what should they say at the funeral.' Just — what do you want to be remembered for?
questions.placeholder: Examples (most people don't need them): 'That I was steady. That my kids never doubted I'd show up.' or 'That I made people laugh.' or 'That I tried to be kind, even when it was inconvenient.'
questions.follow_up_tip: Your Brief will hold this in your own words.

questions.prompt: Specific items for specific people? Things you'd want certain people to have, with the meaning behind them.
questions.placeholder: e.g. Grandfather's watch to Jake — he asked about it every visit since he was eight. Mom's pearls to Lucy.

questions.prompt: One last question. Is there anything you want your family to know — a message, a letter, words you'd want them to find later? Not your wishes about the practical stuff. The other thing. The thing only you can say.
questions.placeholder: Optional. Some people leave this blank and add it later via the Dashboard. Some write a few sentences. Some write a page. Whatever feels right is right.
questions.follow_up_tip: Your Brief will hold this in your words. We'll mark it as the final page so it's the last thing read.
